name: Gareth Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth, 58, an experienced mid-level electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm about average at ordinary wiring and repairs in houses and businesses, not a crew leader or an unusual fault-finding talent. I like getting an old workshop lit evenly, and I use AI occasionally for a checked explanation after a colleague has shown me a method worth trying. What wears me down is being asked to say how long a repair will take before anybody has opened the damaged fitting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household situation at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nina handles warranty claims for an appliance wholesaler, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we have a mortgage on our flat. My wage is typical for the trade, we have two months of expenses saved, and some other electrical firms operate nearby. Our ordinary wages cover the bills, but one Friday next month is already unpaid while a regular customer's workshop is shut, so the margin worries me. I'd like retirement to come into view with real figures, rather than assume my age confirms an income or a stopping date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work the customer still needs the actual repair, whatever became of the grand technology talk. I'd keep a small explanation tool if it earned its place. I'd also ask people not to confuse an ordinary trade year with every worker having an easy paid month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The already unpaid Friday would still worry me, and two months saved isn't money I want to use to cover repeated gaps. My licence is useful, but some nearby firms isn't the same as an offer with enough paid hours. Nina's present claim-handling wage helps cover the bills, and I wouldn't treat it as a spare luxury.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause my pay-as-you-go weekly bowling for eight weeks, cutting 12 a week with no cancellation fee to soften the unpaid Friday. I'd apply for advertised local licensed service jobs within my actual ability now and through the next year. I'd leave only after a signed written offer guaranteed pay and paid hours covering the mortgage and ordinary costs after travel, rather than count an interview as a new wage. My occasional checked AI explanation would remain an ordinary existing habit, not a new learning project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the ordinary pay gap, with something practical to do about spending and applications. I'd miss the bowling more than I'd miss the technology argument. An unpaid Friday is still unpaid when the AI headlines go quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the people you bowl with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I was taking eight weeks off the paid game while a short wage month passed. I could still meet them for a walk or a chat without paying to play. I wouldn't pretend it was a business investment or an automatic new deposit into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another local employer necessarily solve the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd need actual written paid hours and the costs of getting there. A familiar firm name can still offer an unsuitable week. I'd keep the paid work I actually had until an affordable offer was signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the warranty desk is real household work too, not just the wiring job people can photograph. I'd ask for a demonstrated parts-list tool instead of another promise about time saved. I'd also ask workmates whether they wanted to send a clear paid-rota question together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large cut in Nina's claim-handling hours as checking and customer answers move to software over the next few years. My physical service work changes more slowly, though quicker planning could also cut some paid visits. With the already unpaid Friday and two months saved, I'd be awake wondering how we'd cover a large part of her wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask two willing electricians to agree and sign a joint request for a written paid rota before we sent the agreed words to our employer. In the first year I'd practise the approved AI parts-list comparison after a colleague demonstrated it, only free inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained. I'd check every suggested part against the manufacturer's ratings and the job's requirements before using the comparison, not let the aid choose a safe component for me. I'd pause the same fee-free 12 weekly bowling for eight weeks, rather than spend as though Nina's actual paid week couldn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected claim-wage cut, while willing to test a useful tool and ask a question together. I'd sound fairly measured at work and still be doing sums after the lights went out. Knowing how to repair a fitting doesn't tell me how to replace my partner's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if nobody wanted to sign your request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my own paid-rota question without using anybody else's name. The group letter exists only if the people and wording are agreed. I wouldn't call an unanswered request a promise of paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the comparison aid was useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the suggestion with the actual manufacturer's ratings and the job's requirements. A wrong item would be rejected before it reached the work. Faster parts buying isn't useful if the electrician has to undo an unsafe choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd be 60 when thinking AGI arrived and 63 around the capable robot date. Nina's warranty claims face the first date, not the later hands-on one. I'd want actual terms for another paid job, rather than assume an older worker automatically had a retirement route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Nina's claims wage to disappear around 2028 before robots could also reduce my physical repair hours around 2031. Two months saved wouldn't establish a bridge across that gap and the mortgage. I'd lose sleep even though I could still apply for work and ask for actual income figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request available free evening community advice now to check actual resource eligibility, amounts, conditions and dates against our mortgage and ordinary costs. I'd apply for advertised local licensed service jobs within actual ability now and in 2029 if income was still needed. I'd leave only with a signed written offer guaranteeing pay and paid hours covering the mortgage and ordinary costs after travel. The eight-week fee-free bowling pause would remain, and we'd assume no pension entitlement, affordable exit or unoffered money from our grown children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a big part of our income to go before we've confirmed any replacement. I can still choose where to send an application and which question to ask. Having a list of things to do doesn't mean the mortgage has agreed to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the advice service couldn't offer an appointment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what free evening help was actually available elsewhere and keep the unanswered figures marked as unknown. I wouldn't write an imagined payment into the budget while waiting for someone to ring. A request for advice isn't an adviser already sitting at our table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any offer be enough reason to leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the signed pay and guaranteed paid hours would need to cover our actual costs after travel. I'd check the job against my ability then rather than assume the licence made every vacancy suitable. I wouldn't swap an uncertain week for an attractive wage number with no paid hours behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check a practical class and the household figures, not a guarantee that both wages will last. I'd be 63 in 2031 and 66 around the capable robot date in 2034. I'd still separate Nina's claims work from the physical service calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect most of Nina's claims wage to go around the thinking date, and the unknown replacement would keep me awake. The already unpaid Friday is a smaller present reminder that the paid week matters. Extra years give us time to check possible routes without proving either a future job or an affordable exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd enrol in the training centre's two-half-day class on reading modern test-instrument records only if a place was available and the employer paid every fee and travel cost inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained. I'd request available free evening community advice on actual resources, conditions and dates, while keeping current paid electrical service work. In 2032 Nina and I would review confirmed resources, actual costs, ability and real paid options before any exit, requiring affordability and her agreement. I wouldn't count a class as another licence, a job at 64 or a substitute for an actual retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected missing claims wage, though able to examine an ordinary paid-time class rather than rush into buying a new career. I'd sleep better with checked figures, but I wouldn't say I'd stopped worrying before we had them. More preparation time doesn't turn my partner's expected wage loss into a minor inconvenience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would asking the firm about the class mean you had a funded place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the place and the full fee, travel, paid-time and weekly-wage agreement would have to be confirmed before enrolment. If not, I'd keep the existing checked procedures and ask what suitable training was actually available. I wouldn't borrow to make an unfunded class look like a completed plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the 2032 review need to establish before you stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actual amounts, start dates and conditions would have to cover the real household costs, with Nina agreeing the plan. Any paid work option would need an actual offer and the ability to do it then. I'd leave an unknown blank rather than fill it with a child's wages or a pension we hadn't established.

transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends I'd be 68 at thinking AGI and about 71 around the capable robot date. I'd want a checked household choice before either age, not a confident story that everyone my age would be finished with work. I'd still like practical teaching and a paid week I could read now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The already unpaid Friday and possible smaller repair weeks would still worry me over the next few years. Nina's claims work could also lose hours before full AGI, even if the largest change was farther away. Two months saved gives some control, not proof of an affordable exit or a suitable physical job at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the fee-free 12 weekly pay-as-you-go bowling for eight weeks and keep current paid service work with ordinary electrical checks and occasional checked AI explanations. I'd request available free evening community advice now and review actual household records yearly with Nina, sooner if either wage fell. In 2037 we'd check confirmed resources, actual costs, ability and real paid options before any exit, requiring affordability and Nina's agreement. I'd assume no pension amount, automatic help from grown children or work capacity that hadn't actually been established then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the actual next few paid years, though less alarmed by the distant full AGI date. I could still enjoy an evening with the people from bowling even while the paid games were paused. A longer warning doesn't pay for the Friday already missing from my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a grown child's offer settle the retirement question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd discuss any actual offer and what they could afford before counting it, without assuming money, housing or care. I'd want the household plan to say exactly what was agreed. Being a parent doesn't make another adult's wages part of my payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the 2037 figures still left you needing paid work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd check actual ability, actual offers and available support then, with the real shortfall in front of us. I'd count neither a job because I'd once done it nor an income because I'd reached an age. The purpose of checking is to find the missing answer, not to make the page look full.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect most of Nina's claims wage to go before we've confirmed replacement income, with robots reaching my physical work around 2031. Clear paid hours, practical training without lost wages and actual household resource figures would help. I'd like the plan to say who pays the mortgage before it says how brave we're being.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a moderate amount saved means a missed paid day stops mattering. Two months is useful, but I still know which Friday is missing. I can be willing to learn a proven tool and still want the household sum checked by somebody who can explain it.

headlineQuote: I'd like the plan to say who pays the mortgage before it says how brave we're being.
portrait: Gareth, **58**, is an experienced mid-level electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician's licence, doing ordinary wiring and service repairs.
He has **typical pay**, two months saved, some nearby firms and a mortgage, with claims-handler partner Nina and grown children living elsewhere.
An **already unpaid Friday** worries him before AI; expected claims-wage loss drives stronger alarm when thinking work changes quickly.
His **occasional AI use** grows only through demonstrated paid practice, while classes and any later exit remain conditional on real agreements.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** means expected loss of most of Nina's claims wage before confirmed replacement income, followed by physical robot pressure.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear paid hours**, practical training without lost wages and actual household resource figures would support a mortgage plan grounded in confirmed income.
